lines: I find the work your team repeats by hand.
Then I build a system that does it.

parts.text: Below: three examples, how we would start, and who you would talk to.
Three situations I see often. They are illustrations, not named clients. The numbers show the scale, not a promise.

items.title: The Monday report
items.before: Every Monday the operations manager rebuilds the leadership report by hand. Sales come from the accounts system, stock from the warehouse system, deliveries from the courier's website. It takes most of the morning, and the figures are a day old by the meeting.
items.build: The report builds itself overnight from the same three systems and is in the inbox at 7am. The manager reads it, checks anything flagged, and adds comments.
items.result: About 5 hours a week back. Roughly 230 hours a year.

items.title: Setting up a new client
items.before: When a proposal is signed, someone copies the client's details into the customer database (CRM), the billing system and the project tracker. Then they email three colleagues. It takes about 40 minutes a client, and something small is usually missed.
items.build: Signing the proposal starts it. The records appear in all three systems, the right people are told, and anything missing is flagged for a person to fill in.
items.result: At 30 new clients a month, about 20 hours a month back, and no half-set-up accounts.

items.title: Early warning on suppliers
items.before: A distributor found out its main supplier had gone into administration when deliveries stopped. The signs had been public for weeks, in Companies House filings and insolvency notices.
items.build: A system reads those public records every night for the companies you depend on. It emails you the morning something changes, such as overdue accounts or a winding-up petition.
items.result: Weeks of warning instead of none.

items.title: Tenders found too late.
items.text: A competitor met the buyer first.

items.title: One person holds the knowledge.
items.text: They cannot take two weeks off.

sections.head: How we would start
sections.reply: Show me how we would start

items.title: A 30-minute call, free.
items.detail: You tell me where the time goes. I ask how the work actually moves.

items.title: A one-page summary.
items.detail: Where time is lost, what I would automate first, and why. It is yours to keep, whether or not we work together.

items.title: A design you approve.
items.detail: What stays, what changes, what becomes automatic. Nothing changes until you approve it.

items.title: A first system, checked by a person.
items.detail: It does the work and someone checks every result. It runs alone only once the results are consistently right.

items.title: It runs, and reports.
items.detail: You get a regular report of what it did, and of anything it could not do.

parts.text: No sales pitch. If there is nothing worth fixing, I will say so.

sections.head: Who you would talk to
sections.reply: Tell me who I would talk to

parts.text: I am Ruben. I work alone, in London. I have spent years automating work for other organisations.
My main job is running Salesforce at London & Partners. Salesforce is software that companies use to track customers.
When automation fails, the cause is usually how people work together, not the software.
Salesforce certifications: Salesforce Administrator. Salesforce Platform App Builder. Salesforce Agentforce Specialist.
Two questions, both optional. Your answers go into the booking, so I can read them before we talk.

conversation.$: The conversation around the sections. Typed text is matched in this order: a description of the visitor's own work opens the intake with their words in its first field; a question in answers gets that fact; words in a section's intents open that section; anything else gets the fallback.
